title: Loss of SUMOylation drives aberrant PRC1 clustering and 3D genome rewiring independent of H3K27me3.

verified.what_i_actually_checked: Unzipped the journal supplement and parsed both tables in pandas: Table 1 = 11,057 genes with DESeq2 log2 fold change (SUMO RNAi vs control), 0 duplicate FlyBase gene IDs, 2,096 at adjusted p<0.05; Table 2 = 298,674 pairs of chromatin domains (TADs, topologically associating domains) over 1,740 unique domains on 5 chromosome arms, with contact scores in control and SUMO-depleted discs. Computed the key baseline myself: control contact score correlates with SUMO contact score at Pearson r=0.853 (R-squared 0.73), and domain-class means explain only 1.1% of the variance of the change. Downloaded and opened the GEO RNA-seq count table (17,612 genes x 3 control + 3 SUMO replicates) and a CUT&RUN (chromatin profiling) differential report (3,446 regions, 2 replicates per condition); checked file sizes by HTTP HEAD for the Hi-C .mcool maps (280 MB each) and bigwig tracks (14 MB each); read the Zenodo record (code only, GPL-3.0).
verified.what_came_from_paper_text_only: Microscopy and FRAP (fluorescence recovery after photobleaching) condensate measurements and the biophysical polymer modelling are described only in the text and figures; I did not see their source data. The exact formula behind the 'inter-domain contact score' (values from -80 to +98) is not given in the table legend, only that maps were ICE-normalized with cooler/cooltools. The 'noise ceiling' from Hi-C replicates would require reprocessing per-replicate track archives I did not download.

a1_downloadable.note: GEO GSE320399 is public (3 subseries), the 30 MB journal supplement downloads without login, Zenodo code record is open; all verified by download.

a2_label_is_a_column.note: Verified in files: log2Ratio per gene in Supplementary Table 1, and av_score_NOnub / av_score_SUMOnub per domain pair in Supplementary Table 2. No construction needed.

a3_inputs_present.note: Table 2 carries coordinates, distance and chromatin class inline; richer features (CUT&RUN signal per gene or domain) need bigwig processing of ten 14 MB tracks, which is work but not identifier lookups.

a4_units_stated.note: Gene labels are log2 fold change with standard errors, clearly documented. The Hi-C 'contact score' unit/formula is NOT defined in the legend - only ICE normalization is named in methods; partial at best.

a5_enough_rows.note: Verified counts: 298,674 domain pairs and 11,057 genes. But these come from 1,740 domains and a single perturbation contrast (2 control + 3 SUMO Hi-C libraries, 3+3 RNA-seq), so rows are heavily pseudo-replicated.

a6_fits_laptop.working_set: ~0.7 GB (two 280 MB .mcool maps, ten ~14 MB bigwigs, two tables under 30 MB)
a6_fits_laptop.note: Sizes checked by HEAD; everything fits in 16 GB RAM, no GPU needed. Raw Hi-C tar is 5.5 GB and would not be touched.

a7_counts_match_paper.note: Table 2 legend says n=298,674 pairs and I counted exactly that. The paper's '700 differentially expressed genes' reproduces at adjusted p<0.05 and |log2FC|>1.5 (I got 698), though the threshold is unstated.

a8_label_provenance.note: Labels are measurements: DESeq2 output from RNA-seq counts, and contact scores from ICE-normalized Hi-C. No model-derived labels. Trap noted: Table 2's avgLog2Ratio columns are the expression label averaged per domain, so they must never be features when predicting expression.

B1.why: Two clean supplementary tables plus GEO count/report tables; features for a real model need bigwig tracks joined by coordinate.

B2.why: Both xlsx files parsed first try in pandas, but header sits on row 2 and column names carry trailing spaces.

B3.why: All samples processed in one pipeline; DESeq2-normalized expression and ICE-normalized Hi-C, verified in the files.

B4.why: No censored labels; 32,386 of 298,674 rows have missing avgLog2Ratio1 (domains with no assigned genes), counted in file.

B5.why: 0 duplicate gene IDs; only 8 duplicated unordered domain pairs out of 298,674, counted in file.

B6.why: Legend sheets describe every column, but the contact score's formula and units are never defined.

C1.why: Cheap check already done: control score explains 73% of SUMO score, chromatin class explains 1.1% of the change - likely noise.

C2.why: Akita, Orca, C.Origami, Epiphany and a Drosophila epigenome-to-Hi-C model exist and are open; none targets perturbation-induced inter-domain change.

C3.why: Angle is 'nobody has modelled this new dataset', but it is one perturbation in one tissue; weak.

C4.why: Hi-C and CUT&RUN on dissected fly wing discs are costly, but a model would not replace the experiment.

C5.why: Obvious dummy baselines exist and I computed them (control score r=0.853; class-mean R-squared 0.011); paper reports correlations too.

D1.why: Open DNA language models cover fly sequence: Nucleotide Transformer multispecies, HyenaDNA, DNABERT-2.

D2.why: Promoter-scale embeddings for 11,057 genes cache on CPU, but 56 kb median domains exceed most context windows.

D3.why: HyenaDNA and Nucleotide Transformer weights are permissively licensed; the paper's own code is GPL-3.0 on Zenodo.

E1.why: Hold out whole chromosome arms or contiguous domain blocks; chrom columns present in the file.

E2.why: Exactly 5 chromosome arms (311-379 domains each) - the bare minimum number of hold-out groups.

E3.why: Global mean, per-class mean and 'predict the control value' are all computable; I computed two of them.

E4.why: 3 RNA-seq replicates per condition and per-replicate Hi-C tracks exist, so replicate disagreement is estimable with reprocessing.

E5.why: Model must recover PcG domains as H3K27me3/Pc-rich and the r=0.853 control-to-SUMO contact relation.

E6.why: Label shuffling and feature ablation are trivial on a 298,674-row table.

E7.why: No second SUMO-depletion wing-disc dataset found; no year or source column; other fly Hi-C uses different perturbations.

E8.why: I already reproduced the paper's ~700 differentially expressed genes (698) from Supplementary Table 1.

G1.why: FlyBase FBgn gene identifiers in Table 1 and dm6 genome coordinates in Table 2, both seen in file.

G2.why: modENCODE/modERN Drosophila chromatin and transcription-factor ChIP tracks join on dm6 coordinates; FlyBase joins on FBgn.

G3.why: Coordinate overlap of 56 kb domains with many external peaks is many-to-many; needs an aggregation rule.

G4.why: Combined question ('which static features mark rewiring-prone domains') is real but rests on one perturbation.

H1.why: Unchanged genes and unchanged domain pairs are all reported, not just hits; verified in the full tables.

H2.why: One lab, one species, one tissue (wing imaginal disc), one knockdown; stated in methods and visible in GEO sample list.

H3.why: The honest claim is writable in one sentence (see honest_claim_h3).

H4.why: Paper has an explicit 'Limitations and future directions' section naming global SUMO depletion as the key caveat.

I1.why: Cavalli lab (Montpellier) and the Polycomb-condensate / 3D genome community, named on the paper.

I2.why: A predictive model would at best nominate domains for follow-up imaging; unlikely to redirect experiments.

I3.why: No concrete decision attached; correlation or AUC would be reported without a user threshold.

I4.why: The dumbest baselines already capture the structure: control score r=0.853, class means 1.1% of change variance.

J1.why: Real splits and transfer learning possible, but much of the work is bigwig/cool track engineering.

J2.why: Polycomb and Hi-C plausibility judgements need domain intuition; no collaborator identified.

J3.why: A cleaned domain-pair plus chromatin-feature table would be shareable even if the model fails.

J4.why: Scope is bounded (two tables, ten tracks) but no time budget stated.

J5.why: No pre-committed kill date written anywhere for this candidate.

existing_models.name: C.Origami (Tan et al., Nature Biotechnology 2023), a deep network predicting cell-type-specific Hi-C contact maps from DNA sequence plus CTCF binding and chromatin accessibility
existing_models.score_and_split: Reported genome-wide insulation-score correlation on held-out chromosomes in human IMR-90 cells, compared against Akita, DeepC and Orca; it reproduced loss of domains after CTCF depletion in silico.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Transfer to cell types and perturbations outside the training distribution, and identifying trans-acting regulators, are named as open.

existing_models.name: Akita (Fudenberg et al., Nature Methods 2020), a convolutional network predicting 3D folding from 1 Mb of DNA sequence
existing_models.score_and_split: Evaluated on held-out human genomic regions at 2 kb resolution; no fly training data.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Prediction of condition- or perturbation-specific folding changes.

existing_models.name: Epiphany (Yang et al., Genome Biology 2023), predicts Hi-C contact maps from one-dimensional epigenomic signal tracks
existing_models.score_and_split: Held-out chromosomes and cross-cell-line evaluation in human; metrics are map-level correlation and insulation agreement.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Generalizing to unseen cell states and to species beyond human/mouse.

existing_models.name: Drosophila chromatin-folding predictor (Rozenwald et al., PeerJ Computer Science 2020; related to 3DPredictor), gradient boosting and bidirectional LSTM predicting fly TAD folding from ChIP chromatin features
existing_models.score_and_split: Predicts a 'transitional gamma' folding statistic from chromatin marks in fly cell lines; evaluation is within/across cell lines, not perturbation deltas.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Which chromatin factors drive folding causally, and transfer across conditions.

existing_models.name: SVM-MOCCA (Bredesen & Rehmsmeier, Nucleic Acids Research 2019), a support vector machine predicting Drosophila Polycomb response elements from DNA sequence
existing_models.score_and_split: Trained on genome-wide Polycomb binding sites, evaluated for generalization to three independent experimentally defined PRE sets.
existing_models.authors_named_unsolved: Distinguishing active from inactive Polycomb elements in a given tissue.

backbone.name: Nucleotide Transformer multispecies or HyenaDNA (DNA language models with open weights), with gradient boosting on chromatin-track features as the practical baseline
backbone.hardware: CPU laptop; ~11k promoter windows of 2 kb embed and cache in a few hours
backbone.licence: Permissive model weights; paper's own analysis code is GPL-3.0

integration.partner_dataset: modENCODE / modERN Drosophila chromatin and transcription-factor ChIP tracks (dm6), plus FlyBase gene annotation
integration.join_key: dm6 genomic coordinates for domains; FlyBase FBgn identifiers for genes
integration.bigger_question_one_sentence: Do static chromatin and transcription-factor features of a fly TAD predict whether it rewires its long-range contacts when a condensate regulator is removed?

controls.positive_control: The model must recover that PcG-classified domains carry high H3K27me3 and Pc signal, and that control contact score predicts SUMO contact score at r=0.853 (I measured this).
controls.negative_control: Shuffle the contact-change label within chromatin class and confirm collapse to the class mean; ablate the control-score feature.
controls.external_validation: None found: no independent SUMO-depletion wing-disc Hi-C/RNA-seq dataset, and no year or source column for a temporal split.

honest_claim_h3: A model here could claim only: in Drosophila wing imaginal discs from one laboratory, chromatin state and genomic distance explain about 1% of the variance in how inter-domain Hi-C contacts change after a single global SUMO knockdown, with the control contact value explaining most of what is predictable.

plain_idea.one_liner: Use chromatin marks and domain features to predict which fly genome domains change their long-range contacts when SUMO is lost.
plain_idea.train_on: Each example is a pair of chromatin domains (TADs) in the fly genome: 298,674 pairs over 1,740 domains, with genomic distance, chromatin class (Polycomb, Active, Heterochromatin, Null) and the control contact score, verified in the supplementary table.
plain_idea.predict: The change in inter-domain contact score between SUMO-depleted and control wing discs, measured by Hi-C (a method that counts how often two genome regions touch) on 2 control and 3 SUMO-depleted libraries.
plain_idea.why_worthwhile: Polycomb condensate researchers would learn whether 3D rewiring after losing a condensate regulator is predictable from static chromatin features; if it is not, that itself bounds how far feature-based 3D models can go.

more_or_better_data.why: Existing 3D-genome models train on hundreds of human/mouse Hi-C maps; this is 5 fly Hi-C libraries from one tissue and one knockdown. The only novelty is the perturbation, not the scale.

confidence_score.why: Three RNA-seq replicates per condition and per-replicate Hi-C tracks could give a replicate-noise estimate, but the supplementary table only contains merged scores, so the noise model must be rebuilt from raw cool files.

models_beatable.why: C.Origami (2023), Akita (2020) and Epiphany (2023) are not competitors here - they are human/mouse wild-type map predictors and cannot be run on this fly perturbation, so there is no number to beat, only a dummy baseline.

guaranteed_improvement.why: No existing model can be run as our baseline on fly perturbation data, and no joinable new data measures the same inter-domain contact change the same way, so two of the four conditions fail.

ml_idea: Predict, per pair of Drosophila chromatin domains, the change in Hi-C contact score caused by SUMO depletion, from genomic distance, chromatin state and CUT&RUN signal of both domains, with chromosome-arm hold-out; a gene-level variant would predict each gene's log2 expression change from its control chromatin marks and 3D context.

effort.compute_note: Tables were parsed and summarized in under a minute each on this laptop (timed); the 10 hours is for installing pyBigWig/cooler (both missing here) and aggregating ten bigwig tracks plus two 280 MB .mcool maps onto 1,740 domains and 11,057 genes - estimated, not timed.
effort.cheapest_killing_check: Correlate control against SUMO contact score and fit chromatin-class means to the difference. I did this: r=0.853 (73% of variance) and class means explain only 1.1% of the change, so the modelling target is mostly noise.

verdict_reason: Part A passes cleanly in the files - the data downloads, labels are real measured columns (11,057 gene log2 fold changes; 298,674 domain-pair contact scores), counts match the paper, and everything fits a laptop. It dies on Part C (scored 5 of 10, below the 6 threshold) for a reason I verified rather than guessed: the control contact score alone explains 73% of the variance in the SUMO-depleted score, and chromatin class explains just 1.1% of the change, so the prediction target is dominated by noise and regression to the mean. Everything comes from one laboratory, one tissue, one species and one knockdown, there is no second dataset carrying this label for external validation, and the paper itself already reports that mark changes do not correlate with expression changes.
